steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper DSLR on rehearsal-based graph continual learning. Motivate continual learning and catastrophic forgetting, explain what is wrong with how existing methods like ER-GNN fill the replay buffer, introduce our two components (diversity-aware node selection and graph structure learning), and end with a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Continual learning and catastrophic forgetting
2. Categories of continual learning; the rehearsal-based approach and replay buffer
3. ER-GNN and the missing diversity of replayed nodes; coverage-based diversity
4. New issue: low homophily of diverse replayed nodes
5. Proposed model DSLR and its two components
6. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Continual learning
- training new model for every large data stream: time-consuming, costly
- continual learning: learn efficiently from new data without retraining on whole dataset, preserve prior knowledge
- risk: forgetting previous knowledge when training on new data -> performance decline = catastrophic forgetting; goal: mitigate it

2. Approaches
- regularization-based, architectural, rehearsal-based
- rehearsal-based (this paper): store small amount of current-task data for later tasks = replay buffer
- widely recognized as most effective

3. ER-GNN and diversity
- ER-GNN: state-of-the-art rehearsal-based GCL; stores most representative nodes per class
- mean feature (MF): average node features per class, store nodes close to average
- considers class representativeness, overlooks diversity within each class
- Fig. 1 (a): two classes in Citeseer, MF replayed nodes concentrated around class centers -> overfitting risk, worse forgetting
- remedy: coverage-based diversity (CD) -> replayed nodes evenly spread over class embedding space (Fig. 1 (b))

4. Homophily issue
- CD: some replayed nodes near decision boundary connected to many nodes of other classes
- Table 1: CD vs MF -> lower homophily ratio of replayed nodes per class
- low homophily harmful for GNNs (Fig. 2: lower homophily -> more severe forgetting)
- but increase in forgetting performance slows beyond a point, variance increases -> just raising homophily hurts robustness, not effective remedy

5. DSLR
- Diversity enhancement and Structure Learning for Rehearsal-based graph continual learning
- Component 1: select replayed nodes for class representativeness + diversity (CD)
- Component 2: reformulate graph structure so replayed nodes connect to truly informative neighbors (same class = homophily, similar structure = structural proximity)
- CD: diverse nodes covering whole class embedding space -> alleviates forgetting
- few replayed nodes carry old knowledge; irrelevant neighbors hurt performance
- graph structure learning (GSL): add informative neighbors, selectively delete edges; message passing brings high-quality info
- link predictor trained on class labels + graph structure (homophily + structural proximity)
- efficient candidate selection for scalability

6. Contributions
- (1) diversity in replayed node selection, overlooked before
- (2) neighbor quality of replayed nodes strongly affects performance; adopt GSL
- (3) experiments: DSLR beats state-of-the-art GCL methods, even with small replay buffer

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Training a new model for every big stream of new data takes a lot of time and is also expensive. So continual learning has become important for dealing with this challenge. Continual learning focuses on learning efficiently from newly introduced data without retraining the model on the whole dataset, which lets the model keep the knowledge it acquired before. But when the model is trained on new data there is a risk that it forgets the knowledge it acquired before, and the performance declines. This is called catastrophic forgetting, and the ultimate goal of continual learning models is to mitigate it.

Continual learning approaches are broadly divided into the regularization-based approach, the architectural approach, and the rehearsal-based approach. In this paper we investigate the rehearsal-based approach, which stores a small amount of data from the current task to use later when training the next tasks. This collection of data is called the replay buffer. The rehearsal-based approach is widely seen as the most effective one for continual learning compared to the other approaches.

ER-GNN is one of the state-of-the-art rehearsal-based approaches for graph continual learning (GCL). It selects the most representative nodes for each class and stores them in a replay buffer to use later when training the next tasks. Specifically, ER-GNN proposed the mean feature (MF) approach, which computes the average of the node features in each class and stores the nodes that are close to the average of each class in the replay buffer. This approach considers how representative of the class each replayed node is, but we argue that it overlooks the diversity of the replayed nodes within each class. Fig. 1 (a) shows nodes from two different classes in the Citeseer dataset and the replayed nodes for each class obtained with MF. We see that the replayed nodes for each class are mostly concentrated around the center of each class in the embedding space. This creates a potential risk of overfitting to the nodes in those regions, which makes catastrophic forgetting worse. As a simple remedy that considers both the class representativeness and the diversity within each class of the replayed nodes, we devise a coverage-based diversity (CD) approach for selecting the nodes to replay. With this, the replayed nodes can be spread evenly across the embedding space of each class (See Fig. 1 (b)), which means that overfitting to specific regions can be alleviated.

Homophily issue
- CD: some replayed nodes near decision boundary connected to many nodes of other classes
- Table 1: CD vs MF -> lower homophily ratio of replayed nodes per class
- low homophily harmful for GNNs (Fig. 2: lower homophily -> more severe forgetting)
- but increase in forgetting performance slows beyond a point, variance increases -> just raising homophily hurts robustness

DSLR
- Diversity enhancement and Structure Learning for Rehearsal-based graph continual learning
- Component 1: replayed node selection for class representativeness + diversity (CD)
- Component 2: reformulate graph structure -> truly informative neighbors (homophily + structural proximity)
- few replayed nodes carry old knowledge; irrelevant neighbors hurt performance
- GSL: add informative neighbors, selectively delete edges; message passing
- link predictor on class labels + graph structure; efficient candidate selection for scalability

Contributions
- (1) diversity in replayed node selection, overlooked before
- (2) neighbor quality of replayed nodes strongly affects performance; adopt GSL
- (3) DSLR beats state-of-the-art GCL methods, even with small replay buffer

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Training a new model for every big stream of new data takes a lot of time and is also expensive. So continual learning has become important for dealing with this challenge. Continual learning focuses on learning efficiently from newly introduced data without retraining the model on the whole dataset, which lets the model keep the knowledge it acquired before. But when the model is trained on new data there is a risk that it forgets the knowledge it acquired before, and the performance declines. This is called catastrophic forgetting, and the ultimate goal of continual learning models is to mitigate it.

Continual learning approaches are broadly divided into the regularization-based approach, the architectural approach, and the rehearsal-based approach. In this paper we investigate the rehearsal-based approach, which stores a small amount of data from the current task to use later when training the next tasks. This collection of data is called the replay buffer. The rehearsal-based approach is widely seen as the most effective one for continual learning compared to the other approaches.

ER-GNN is one of the state-of-the-art rehearsal-based approaches for graph continual learning (GCL). It selects the most representative nodes for each class and stores them in a replay buffer to use later when training the next tasks. Specifically, ER-GNN proposed the mean feature (MF) approach, which computes the average of the node features in each class and stores the nodes that are close to the average of each class in the replay buffer. This approach considers how representative of the class each replayed node is, but we argue that it overlooks the diversity of the replayed nodes within each class. Fig. 1 (a) shows nodes from two different classes in the Citeseer dataset and the replayed nodes for each class obtained with MF. We see that the replayed nodes for each class are mostly concentrated around the center of each class in the embedding space. This creates a potential risk of overfitting to the nodes in those regions, which makes catastrophic forgetting worse. As a simple remedy that considers both the class representativeness and the diversity within each class of the replayed nodes, we devise a coverage-based diversity (CD) approach for selecting the nodes to replay. With this, the replayed nodes can be spread evenly across the embedding space of each class (See Fig. 1 (b)), which means that overfitting to specific regions can be alleviated.

But we observed that putting emphasis on diversity with CD can cause another issue: some replayed nodes (i.e., the ones near the decision boundary as shown in Fig. 1 (b)) will inevitably be connected to many nodes from different classes. Concretely, Table 1 shows that using CD instead of MF gives a lower homophily ratio of the replayed nodes for each class. This then results in a low homophily ratio of the replayed nodes, and this is harmful for training Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), since their performance is known to degrade on graphs with a low homophily ratio (See Fig. 2 where the replayed nodes with a lower homophily make the model forget previously acquired knowledge more severely). On the other hand, it is important to note that the increase in the forgetting performance starts to slow down after a certain point, and the variance starts to increase. This shows that simply increasing the homophily ratio of the replay buffer makes the model less robust, so it is not an effective remedy.

Because of these issues with the replay buffer of rehearsal-based approaches for GCL, we propose a GCL model called Diversity enhancement and Structure Learning for Rehearsal-based graph continual learning (DSLR). It has two major components: Component 1 – selecting the replayed nodes so that both the class representativeness and the diversity within each class are considered, and Component 2 – reformulating the graph structure so that the replayed nodes are encouraged to be connected to truly informative neighbors. We define truly informative neighbors as neighbors that both belong to the same class as the target node (i.e., homophily) and share a similar structure (i.e., structural proximity).

More precisely, for Component 1 we devise a coverage-based diversity (CD) approach for selecting the nodes to replay. The main idea of CD is to select diverse nodes while also considering the class representativeness, so that the replayed nodes represent the whole embedding space of their own classes well, and this helps alleviate catastrophic forgetting. On the other hand, the rehearsal-based approach relies heavily on a few replayed nodes to keep the knowledge from previous tasks, so if replayed nodes that have irrelevant neighbors are involved in model training, this can have a significant detrimental impact on model performance. To address this, we adopt graph structure learning (GSL) to reformulate the graph structure so that the replayed nodes can be connected to truly informative neighbors, and high-quality information can then be propagated into the replayed nodes through message passing (Component 2). The main idea of GSL is to add informative neighbors to the replayed nodes and to selectively delete edges between the replayed nodes and their neighbors, and both of these help make the replay buffer more effective. More precisely, we train a link predictor using both the class labels and the graph structure to capture homophily and structural proximity, respectively, and this helps us find truly informative neighbors of the replayed nodes. Last, we also devise an efficient candidate selection method to make the graph structure learning more scalable.

Our contributions are:

- (1) We emphasize considering diversity when selecting the replayed nodes, which existing methods have overlooked, so that the replayed nodes can represent the whole data of their class effectively.

- (2) We present a new discovery that the quality of the neighbors around the replayed nodes has a substantial influence on the overall model performance. For this, we adopt graph structure learning to make sure the replayed nodes are connected to truly informative neighbors.

- (3) Extensive experiments show that DSLR outperforms state-of-the-art GCL methods, even when the replay buffer is small.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Training a new model for every large stream of new data is both time-consuming and cost-intensive. Hence, continual learning [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8] has become crucial in addressing this challenge. Continual learning emphasizes efficient learning from newly introduced data without retraining the model on the entire dataset, enabling previously acquired knowledge to be preserved. However, when the model is trained on new data, there is a risk of forgetting the previously acquired knowledge, resulting in a performance decline. This phenomenon is referred to as catastrophic forgetting, and the ultimate goal of continual learning models is to mitigate it.

Continual learning approaches are broadly categorized into the regularization-based approach [9,10,11,12,6], the architectural approach [2], and the rehearsal-based approach [4,13,6,14,7]. The rehearsal-based approach, which we investigate in this paper, stores a small amount of data from the current task for later use when training subsequent tasks. This collection of data is referred to as the replay buffer. The rehearsal-based approach is widely recognized as the most effective among the approaches for continual learning [15].

One of the state-of-the-art rehearsal-based approaches for graph continual learning (GCL), ER-GNN [7], selects the most representative nodes for each class and stores them in a replay buffer for later use in training subsequent tasks. Specifically, ER-GNN proposed the mean feature (MF) approach, which computes the average of the node features in each class and stores nodes close to each class average in the replay buffer. However, while this approach considers the class representativeness of each replayed node, we argue that it overlooks the diversity of the replayed nodes within each class. Fig. 1 (a) shows nodes belonging to two different classes in the Citeseer dataset, along with the replayed nodes for each class obtained using MF. We observe that the replayed nodes for each class are mainly concentrated around the center of each class in the embedding space, incurring a potential risk of overfitting to nodes in those regions, which aggravates catastrophic forgetting. As a simple remedy that considers both the class representativeness and the diversity within each class of the replayed nodes, we devise a coverage-based diversity (CD) approach for selecting nodes to be replayed. In this way, the replayed nodes are evenly distributed across the embedding space of each class (See Fig. 1 (b)), so overfitting to specific regions can be alleviated.

However, we observed that emphasizing diversity using CD can lead to another issue: some replayed nodes (i.e., those near the decision boundary as shown in Fig. 1 (b)) are inevitably connected to many nodes from different classes. Concretely, Table 1 shows that using CD instead of MF leads to a lower homophily ratio of the replayed nodes for each class. This results in a low homophily ratio of the replayed nodes, which is harmful for training Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), whose performance is known to degrade on graphs with a low homophily ratio [16,17] (See Fig. 2, where replayed nodes with lower homophily cause the model to forget previously acquired knowledge more severely). On the other hand, it is important to note that the increase in the forgetting performance begins to slow down beyond a certain point, while the variance begins to increase. This indicates that simply increasing the homophily ratio of the replay buffer deteriorates model robustness and is therefore not an effective remedy.

In light of these issues regarding the replay buffer of rehearsal-based approaches for GCL, we propose a GCL model named Diversity enhancement and Structure Learning for Rehearsal-based graph continual learning (DSLR), which consists of two major components: Component 1 – selecting the replayed nodes so as to consider both the class representativeness and the diversity within each class, and Component 2 – reformulating the graph structure to encourage the replayed nodes to be connected to truly informative neighbors. We define truly informative neighbors as those that not only belong to the same class as the target node (i.e., homophily), but also share a similar structure (i.e., structural proximity).

More precisely, we devise a coverage-based diversity (CD) approach for selecting nodes to be replayed (Component 1). The main idea of CD is to select diverse nodes while considering class representativeness, ensuring that the replayed nodes effectively represent the entire embedding space of their own classes, which helps alleviate catastrophic forgetting. On the other hand, since the rehearsal-based approach relies heavily on a few replayed nodes to retain knowledge from previous tasks, involving replayed nodes with irrelevant neighbors in model training may significantly harm model performance. To address this, we adopt graph structure learning (GSL) [18,17,19] to reformulate the graph structure so that the replayed nodes are connected to truly informative neighbors, allowing high-quality information to be propagated into the replayed nodes through message passing (Component 2). The main idea of GSL is to add informative neighbors to the replayed nodes and selectively delete edges between replayed nodes and their neighbors, both of which enhance the effectiveness of the replay buffer. More precisely, we train a link predictor using both the class labels and the graph structure to capture homophily and structural proximity, respectively, which helps us discover truly informative neighbors of the replayed nodes. Finally, we devise an efficient candidate selection method to improve the scalability of graph structure learning.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- (1) We emphasize the importance of diversity when selecting the replayed nodes, a factor overlooked in existing methods, to ensure that replayed nodes effectively represent the entire data of their respective class.

- (2) We present a novel discovery about the substantial influence of the quality of neighbors surrounding the replayed nodes on overall model performance. To this end, we adopt graph structure learning so that the replayed nodes are connected to truly informative neighbors.

- (3) Extensive experiments show that DSLR outperforms state-of-the-art GCL methods, even with a small replay buffer size.
